newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbia faces growing criticism over crackdown.
newsitem.headline: Serbia faces growing criticism over crackdown.

text.p: Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic faced a growing chorus of international criticism after his government cracked down on more than five weeks of street protests against his rule.
But one of his ministers rejected Western condemnation as a misguided and ill-informed attempt to interfere in the Balkan republic's internal affairs.

The United States led demands for the Serbian authorities to show restraint and not interfere with democratic rights of demonstrators. "We continue to hold Milosevic responsible for any violence which may occur," the State Department said.
Germany also warned Milosevic not to hinder the street protests which have been held every day since he refused to accept a stunning series of opposition victories in local elections on November 17.

A delegation from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) which visited Belgrade at Milosevic's invitation last weekend was expected to issue its findings on Friday on the alleged electoral fraud.
Both the government and opposition have said the OSCE's findings would not be binding, but its report was likely to back the opposition and add to international pressure on Milosevic.
German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said the outside world would not stand by if Milosevic banned opposition political rallies in Belgrade on the grounds that they obstructed traffic.

"President Milosevic has to be aware of the fact that the world is keeping its eyes on Belgrade," Kinkel said. "He should keep his hands off the demonstrators' rights and their freedom to congregate. A further escalation won't be tolerated."
Although no states have been specific about what action they may take, they have spoken of economic and diplomatic reprisals depriving Serbia of desperately-needed links with the West.

France and Italy both expressed concern over street violence in Belgrade, while Britain said it had told the Yugoslav Foreign Ministry that it risked damaging prospects for improved international relations.
Riot police took action on Thursday to push opposition demonstrators off the streets to enforce an Interior Ministry ban on marches for disrupting traffic.
"We deplore today's attempts by the Serbian authorities to impede the right of the opposition to demonstrate peacefully," a British Embassy statement said.

Marches by supporters of the Zajedno opposition coalition had passed off without violence for five weeks but Milosevic's ruling Socialist Party organised a counter-demonstration on Tuesday that touched off street fighting.
The West accused Milosevic of provoking the clashes by scheduling the counter-rally at the same time and place as the regular Zajedno demonstration.

Deputy Prime Minister Nikola Sainovic rejected the charge. "On one day for one hour at a legally-announced place, we gathered supporters of President Milosevic and these others (opposition supporters) attacked them," he said.
"I think that the Western allegations are worthless given the facts that speak quite contrary to the accusations."
He said the authorities would not use force against demonstrators but added: "Anyone who violates or questions the authority of the law will not be tolerated."

Thousands of riot police moved into central Belgrade to enforce the Interior Ministry ban. They ignored a march through snow-covered streets by 5,000 students but were firm with around 30,000 Zajedno activists blocking a main street.
They backed the demonstrators into a pedestrian area at the nearby Republic Square, butting those who resisted with their shields and hitting them with batons but without severe force.
Zajedno leaders stepped up their rhetoric after this week's violence and now speak of a potential for open conflict.

"Can you imagine a country in which, after losing local elections, its president tries to provoke a civil war?" asked opposition leader Zoran Djindjic. "Can you imagine what he would do if he lost a presidential election -- provoke a world war?"
